2.text: where they asked the natives for these. As mentioned above, the Kolyma

3.text: River, which for the last fifty years has known no sables, abounded at that

4.text: time, on the contrary, in the best, very dark sable. According to Slovtzov,

5.text: in the eighteenth century the fair of Sredne-Kolymsk brought to the treasury

6.text: as the usual tithe ninety doublescores¹ of sables. Therefore the whole number

7.text: of sables brought to the fair was about thirty-six thousand.

8.text: The Anadyr River, on the other hand, as may be seen from the reports

9.text: quoted above, even in earlier times, had no sables because of the scarcity

10.text: of wood. In the first years, however, the Cossacks succeeded in extorting

11.text: from the natives a considerable number of sable-skins, whole and split, pro-

12.text: bably acquired by the natives from their southern neighbors. On the Anadyr

13.text: River and to the north of Kolymsk, the Cossacks turned their attention to

14.text: walrus-tusks, which were also of great value. According to a record con-

15.text: tained in one of the reports mentioned, fourteen sables were equivalent to

16.text: one pud of walrus-ivory; so that the fifty puds of walrus-ivory mentioned

17.text: above were equivalent to seven hundred sables; i.e., to seventeen double-

18.text: scores and a half of sable-peltries. Numerous decrees of the Government were

19.text: issued in reference to the quality of the tribute to be collected from the na-

20.text: tives. Most of them say, “You have to take good and whole sables, without

21.text: bare spots, with tails and with bellies; and you must not take as Czar’s

22.text: tribute sables not whole, and with bare spots, or rotten and torn ones, and

23.text: not full-haired. You have to take the tribute and presents and enter them

24.text: in the tribute-books, year after year, and one name after another. You have

25.text: to take of walrus-tusks, as tribute, only the best, and of medium size. Small

26.text: tusks, weighing less than one pound each, you must not take for tribute.”

27.text: A great number of natives were exterminated by the conquerors. The

28.text: reports are full of remarks like the following: “The village was taken, and

29.text: all the people put to death.” The natives defended themselves with the courage

30.text: of despair; but in the contests, they could do no more than kill a few of

31.text: the assailants. Then they had to give way before steel blades and fire-arms.

32.text: Those that were left alive promised to pay tribute, and gave the best men

33.text: as hostages. The Cossacks, however, were quite far from enjoying their

34.text: position. The northern clime and the conditions of life were too severe even

35.text: for those adventurers. Thus one report says, “We live on dead red-fish

36.text: [several species of Oncorhyncus, such as O. keta, O. niarka, O. gorbusha].

37.text: Of white-fish we catch but little, because we have no good nets. We do

38.text: not dare to feed the Czar’s hostages with that dead fish, lest they die from

39.text: scurvy: so we spare the white-fish and feed them with that.” Another report

40.text: says, “We are starving to death, we feed on cedar-bark. Whatever fish was

41.text: left we spared for the hostages, and portioned that off to them.”

42.text: Along with war came trade with the natives. Thus, in the year 1646
